newsitem.title: USA: Jewell in movie talks with Fox, HBO - attorneys.
newsitem.headline: Jewell in movie talks with Fox, HBO - attorneys.

text.p: Former Olympic bomb suspect Richard Jewell has been talking possible movie deals with Hollywood studios including Rupert Murdoch's 20th Century Fox and Ted Turner's HBO, his attorneys said on Monday.
But the 34-year-old former security guard was not close to signing a contract, they said, despite a press report that Fox was near an agreement involving an offer of around $500,000.

"We're interested in seeing his story told -- correctly -- by anybody who intends to tell it," said G. Watson Bryant, the Atlanta attorney who heads Jewell's legal team. "Right now, we have no deal. If you want to characterise it as being close to signing a deal, I think you're being a little aggressive."
The Hollywood journal Daily Variety said TriStar, owned by Sony Corp., HBO and the 20th Century Fox studio, Fox 2000, had bid on rights to a movie deal with Jewell.

Quoting unnamed sources, it said Fox was close to "a mid-six-figure deal" for the life rights of Jewell, his mother Bobi and his legal team. The package also would include rights to "American Nightmare: The Ballad of Richard Jewell," an article in the February issue of Vanity Fair magazine.

In the Vanity Fair article, author Marie Brenner got exclusive access to Jewell, his family and attorneys and detailed how the life of a simple man was quickly disrupted by the media and the FBI, which hounded Jewell and tore apart his house but never found any evidence.

Daily Variety said Fox, part of the business empire controlled by Australian-born media mogul Rupert Murdoch, was close to prevailing over HBO because it was willing to spend slightly more upfront money and because Jewell and his lawyers were interested in seeing his story made into a feature.
A Fox spokeswoman declined to comment on the report.
HBO is owned by Time Warner Inc. and run by Time Warner vice chairman Ted Turner, Cable News Network founder.

Jewell's attorneys say they would be eager to see a Hollywood film showing how their client became a suspect in the July 27, 1996, Centennial Olympic Park bombing that rocked Atlanta at the height of the Summer Games, leaving two people dead and more than 100 injured.
From the day he was named a suspect in a special edition of the Atlanta Journal newspaper, Jewell spent nearly three months being hounded by federal agents and news cameras.
The Justice Department publicly cleared him of all suspicion in the case last October, and his legal team has since forged ahead with plans to sue members of the media and individual FBI agents.
Th Wall Street Journal said Jewell reached an out-of-court settlement worth more than $500,000 with the NBC television network, which is owned by General Electric Co.

"There's no question that we think the American public needs to know what happened to Richard Jewell and who did this to him. And that's why we do have an interest in his story being told on a national basis," said Lin Wood, one of two civil attorneys representing Jewell.
